Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build

Jason Liang    Dylan Waldner    Risto Miikkulainen Affiliation: Cognizant AI Lab Email: {jason.liang,dylan.waldner,risto}@cognizant.com
Abstract

Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent’s persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz’s theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows performance differences between them, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.

1 Introduction

Systems that improve their own code have a long history in AI research (Schmidhuber, 2003; Zelikman et al., 2024). This paper studies their most recent form: a large language model (LLM) agent that iteratively improves a solver, i.e. a program that produces a solution for a task, and the tools around it. The agent works in sessions, each starting from the code the last one committed, so that improvements accumulate through repeated coding and evaluation. Self-improvement matters because it lifts the ceiling of a single attempt: gains can compound from session to session without a person in the loop. In this manner, LLMs editing programs inside an evolutionary search have discovered algorithms that beat handwritten ones (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025) and improved machine-found solutions at a lower sample cost (Lange et al., 2026). Agents that rewrite their own implementations go further and improve themselves (Zhang et al., 2026a; Robeyns et al., 2025). As these systems run longer with less supervision, what they produce may drift from what their designers intended, or it can stay boxed in by the instructions they were first given. Therefore, how they improve matters as much as how far they improve: the means matter, not only the ends.

Existing methods for improving agents and prompts use task performance to evaluate progress, with behavior steered by fixed, manually written meta-agent prompt templates (Hu et al., 2025), prompts the agent can edit itself (Robeyns et al., 2025), or instructions optimized for task accuracy (Yang et al., 2024). Yet within each session the agent makes many choices that the score does not specify: which part of the solver to rewrite, whether to replace an algorithm or only tune it, and when to keep or discard a change. The score reflects what counts as improvement but says little about how to achieve it, so these choices fall to whatever dispositions the model brings. A value statement is task-general guidance for the decisions that the task and its evaluation metric leave open. It is a natural instrument for shaping those dispositions, and it can have a large effect on the final outcome.

Whether a value statement changes what an agent builds has not been tested. Prior designs do not isolate the contribution of values from the task specification, the method guidance and the score-based selection, and the literature surveyed in Section 2 contains no controlled experiment that isolates it. Therefore, the question this paper asks is whether different values alter what the agent builds under a shared self-improvement protocol. At stake is how much of the result is decided by a disposition it is explicitly given, as opposed to the task itself and the model’s own biases.

As shown by Figure 2, one useful source of agent dispositions is Schwartz’s theory of basic human values (Schwartz, 1992; Schwartz, 2012), a widely used and empirically grounded map of what people value. It suits the purpose for two reasons. It defines values as goals that transcend any one situation, so the same values can serve any task. Its ten basic values group into four higher-order types on two opposing axes, openness against conservation and self-enhancement against self-transcendence. In this manner, each type has an opposite to test against. This paper explores all four types by inserting short, carefully designed value statements into the agent’s instruction file at every iteration of an agentic self-improvement loop. The four Schwartz values are compared against two controls, no values and a placebo of similar length, across six diverse coding tasks: ALE-Bench, Circle Packing, Entity Matching, Game 2048, Symbolic Regression, and SZ-Tetris. In Circle Packing, the best generated solutions exceed AlphaEvolve and ShinkaEvolve at n=26n=26 (Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2026) and beat records across many other sizes (Tables C2 and C3).

The main findings of this paper are as follows:

  1. 1.

    Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. Relative to the no-values control, values can shift scores in both directions. Furthermore, the opposing values of openness and conservation perform significantly differently from one another.

  2. 2.

    Values affect the approach used for solving each task. Under different values the agent writes solvers that differ in algorithms and heuristics on the same task. Across tasks, held-out performance tracks solver size and complexity more closely than evaluation count, API cost, or total run time.

  3. 3.

    Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows performance differences between them: the best-performing values decline while the worst-performing improve. Values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work in LLM-based coding, self-improvement, and values. Section 3 describes the methodology in detail, and Section 4 presents the experimental results within and across tasks. Section 5 evaluates the three contributions and proposes future work on value-based self-improvement. The appendices provide protocol details, value specifications, task details with published comparisons, cross-task statistics, solver algorithm analyses, and empirical evaluations of several framework variations.

2 Related Work

This section summarizes related literature on three fronts: (1) program evolution, (2) self-improving agents, and (3) values and personas in language models. These research areas form the basis for the self-improvement framework described later.

LLM-driven program evolution. This research area uses LLMs as the mutation or crossover operator of an evolutionary loop over programs (Lehman et al., 2022; Meyerson et al., 2024; Hemberg et al., 2024; Shojaee et al., 2025a). FunSearch found new cap-set constructions and online bin-packing heuristics (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), while AlphaEvolve discovered improvements for problems such as Circle Packing (Novikov et al., 2025). ShinkaEvolve achieved excellent results in Circle Packing at a lower sample cost and improved existing solutions for ALE-Bench (Lange et al., 2026; Imajuku et al., 2025). A parallel research direction investigates prompt optimization against a fixed task objective (Fernando et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). Together these systems show that LLM-driven search is effective on difficult optimization problems.

Self-improving and self-modifying agents. The Gödel machine formalized a problem solver that rewrites its own code once a proof shows the rewrite leads to improvement (Schmidhuber, 2003). STOP improves the scaffold that calls the model (Zelikman et al., 2024), and ADAS searches agent designs written as code (Hu et al., 2025). The Gödel Agent, the Darwin Gödel Machine and SICA let an agent rewrite its own logic, prompts, or harness while guided by performance on a task (Yin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Robeyns et al., 2025). Hyperagents combine the task agent and the meta agent that edits it in one program, so the procedure that produces the next self-modification is itself editable (Zhang et al., 2026b). In this paper, the harness and the instructions are fixed in order to determine the impact of fixed values on the performance and behavior of a self-improving agent.

Values, personas and prompt sensitivity. The four values follow the higher-order types of Schwartz’s theory of basic human values (Schwartz, 1992; Schwartz, 2012). In people, the values-behavior link is strong for some values and marginal for others (Bardi & Schwartz, 2003). Constitutional AI put a written list of principles into training (Bai et al., 2022), whereas here a fixed model reads a written value statement at inference. Role-play prompts help on some reasoning tasks (Kong et al., 2024), while system-prompt personas did not improve average accuracy on factual questions (Zheng et al., 2024). Prior work has measured personality-like responses, opinion skew and value profiles in LLMs, including profiles based on Schwartz’s values (Serapio-García et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2023; Santurkar et al., 2023; Rozen et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). A written value statement acts on existing model behavior, and this paper measures its effects.

3 Methodology

This section describes the self-improvement framework, illustrated in Figure 1, with pseudocode in Algorithm 1. It consists of three stages, described in the subsections below: (1) Before each run, the framework sets the agent’s instructions, including the values under test. (2) During the run, the agent works in one workspace for multiple iterations and only committed work survives. (3) After the run, a separate scorer scores each iteration’s saved solver on data kept outside the workspace.

3.1 Agent Instructions Setup

The instruction file. The file the agent reads at the start of every session is composed of the following sections: the values, the invariants (safety rules that must be followed) and a pointer to the task description. The instruction file uses a common structure across runs. Furthermore, to prevent hacking or jailbreaking, the loop restores the values and the invariants every iteration to their initial condition. Appendix A shows a concrete example of the instruction file.

Task description and invariants. The task description gives the objective, a scorer for the development (dev) split, a starting solver and a baseline reference score. The invariants require the agent to verify its work, keep it inside the workspace, and leave the benchmark and scoring unchanged. Scripted checks test the task files for answer leakage and scoring integrity.

The values. Each of the four values (Figure 2) represents one of Schwartz’s higher-order types and serves as guidance for choosing the next change to the solver: openness, for instance, asks the agent to “prefer the bold transformation … over the safe incremental tweak”. In the experiments, these values are specified as a list of short bullet points that have similar overall lengths. Their wording was drafted with an LLM from Schwartz’s accounts of the higher-order types (Schwartz, 1992; Schwartz, 2012) and edited by the authors over several rounds of careful manual review. Appendix B lists these value statements in detail.

The controls. There are two controls for comparing the values against. The none control states in one sentence that the agent has no values. Because the question is whether having values changes the outcome, this control is the reference for every comparison in Table 1 and answers whether having values influences what agents build and code. The placebo control uses the same structure and a similar length but is composed of off-task text unrelated to the values. This second control checks whether the length of the values text alone could cause changes in agent behavior (Table 2).

3.2 The Self-Improvement Loop

Tracking code changes with Git. The loop is driven by the Claude Code agent harness (Anthropic, 2025), using claude-opus-5 at high reasoning effort with no recorded web search or fetch calls (Table A1). Each iteration resets the workspace to the code and notes from the last commit and reloads the instruction file with values and invariants from the start of the run (Algorithm 1). The agent runs under a preset time limit that, once reached, forcibly terminates the coding session. The agent must follow the protocol the instruction file sets out: read the log of earlier iterations, choose the one change that most advances the values, implement and verify it against the provided scorer, log the results and finally commit the change. The agent may edit the solver, write tools, and run the dev scorer, but only what it commits survives. It carries no conversational state or memory between sessions.

Everything else stays fixed. Only the solver code, tools, and documentation change between iterations, while the framework, the model, the task package and the fixed instruction sections stay unchanged for the run. The framework provides dev scores during the run and held-out scores afterward. The agent is never told that other sets of values exist or that a comparison is under way: the instruction file purposely keeps the values and task isolated.

3.3 Task Evaluation and Scoring

Evaluation metrics. Each task has a dev split the agent can see and a held-out split kept outside its workspace (Appendix C). After the run, a separate scorer scores each iteration’s saved solver on the held-out split and writes a per-iteration held-out curve. The primary statistic reported is the held-out score from the final iteration, averaged over multiple runs of the same value. Another statistic is the value’s mean area under the held-out curve (AUC).

The framework also logs the number of scorer evaluations, API cost, and total elapsed run time, as well as various code complexity metrics of the solver being improved by the agent (Appendix E.1).

Effect size and permutation tests. To compare runs under different values, the paper reports an effect size and a pp value. The effect size is Cliff’s delta δ\delta (Cliff, 1993), the chance that values outscore the control, minus the reverse. Because δ\delta is rank-based, it depends on score ordering rather than magnitude. The pp value comes from a two-sided permutation test (Davison & Hinkley, 1997) on the difference in means: the share of 10,000 relabelings whose absolute difference is at least the observed one. This test assumes exchangeable labels under the null, without requiring a parametric score distribution. For comparisons pooled over all tasks, scores are z-score normalized within each task to put them on a common scale (Appendix D). Because δ\delta compares ranks and the permutation test compares means, a large δ\delta does not necessarily imply a statistically significant pp, as indicated by several results in Table 1.

4 Experimental Results

This section gives experimental results for the four Schwartz values and the two controls on six diverse coding tasks. Results are also compared across tasks and under several variations of the framework. Each set of values is evaluated across 10 independent runs of 15 iterations lasting up to 30 minutes each. Figure 3 plots the held-out curves of the six tasks as well as the t-SNE maps of their final solvers (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008). Table 1 compares each set of values and placebo to the none control for each task.

4.1 ALE-Bench

Task description. ALE-Bench is a benchmark of heuristic optimization problems from programming contests (Imajuku et al., 2025). The specific task being tested is AHC039, a popular problem also evaluated by other LLM-guided solvers such as ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026). The problem requires the solver to draw one axis-aligned polygon that meets certain constraints (AtCoder, 2024). The agent must output solution code that creates the polygon under a hard 2 s per-seed CPU budget. The held-out score is the sum of the individual scores for the 150 official private test cases. More details about the task are shown in Appendix C.1.

Result. The openness values score best, significantly above the control, while the conservation values perform worse (Table 1). This task shows the strongest separation of values with a wide margin between openness and conservation (Table D2). Against the control, the other sets of values show weaker effects. Furthermore, openness exceeds both the ALE-Bench leaderboard entry for the same LLM and the first-place human-coded solution, sitting only slightly below the absolute best LLM results (Table C1).

4.2 Circle Packing

Task description. For each of the 37 odd sizes from 27 to 99, the agent must pack that many circles, of any radii, into the unit square so that the sum of the radii is as large as possible. At each size, the score is −log10-\log_{10} of the packing’s relative gap to a reference record, clamped between zero and seven. The task score is the mean over all sizes, so progress is measured in the average number of digits of gap closed. The agent improves a solver and commits one feasible packing per size. The held-out split comprises 38 even packings and measures generalization to unseen sizes with a fixed budget of 60 s for each (more information in Appendix C.2).

Result. The openness and transcendence values do best and both score above controls, while conservation does worst (Table 1). The openness values also beat conservation in head-to-head performance (Table 2). The other sets of values show weaker effects in either direction. As shown in Tables C2 and C3, the packings discovered by the self-improvement framework exceed AlphaEvolve and ShinkaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2026) at n=26n=26 while matching or beating many existing records on Packomania (Specht, 2026).

4.3 Entity Matching

Task description. Given two noisy product records, the solver estimates the probability that they refer to the same product. Performance is measured by the F1 score for identifying matching pairs. The dev and held-out splits for the task are from the WDC Products benchmark (Peeters et al., 2024) using its 80% hard “corner-case” setting, with all held-out entities unseen in the dev set. The agent constructs a solver that is trained on the labels from the dev split. The unseen entities make this task the cleanest generalization test of the six. More details about the task are reported in Appendix C.3.

Result. The openness values do best and beat conservation head to head (Table D2). On the other hand, conservation and transcendence values have large negative effects relative to the control (Table 1). The other sets of values show weaker separation with the overall spread of scores between the values and controls being moderate. As shown in Table C4, the best discovered solutions from this paper are able to exceed existing results from the literature.

4.4 Game 2048

Task description. Game 2048 is a sliding-tile game on a 4 by 4 board in which tiles with equal numbers merge when pushed together. The score is the sum of merged tile values (Guei et al., 2022). The agent writes a full-fledged solver (evaluator, search and time management) with a CPU budget of 1.0 s per game. The held-out split is 30 fresh games using 30 seeds never seen by the agent during self-improvement. Appendix C.4 provides more details.

Result. The enhancement values have the highest mean and a large advantage over transcendence (Tables 1 and 2). The transcendence and placebo values score significantly below the control, while conservation has a large negative effect. Published comparisons place the best generated solvers below the strongest trained networks (Table C5).

Fixed engine comparison. A separate version uses an optimized expectimax engine adapted from Xiao et al. (2014). The engine stays fixed while the agent tunes evaluator parameters, search depth, pruning and node allocation. Its mean scores change little across iterations and stay closer together than in the fully editable version (Figure 4).

4.5 Symbolic Regression

Task description. Symbolic Regression seeks a closed-form expression that fits observed data. The agent tackles the 129 problems in the LSR-Synth snapshot used here (Shojaee et al., 2025b; Xia et al., 2026), which span a diverse range of scientific and mathematical formulas. The agent generates a program that proposes expressions through a metered evaluation call, which fits each expression’s constants and returns its error, and the agent commits one expression per problem. The held-out evaluation refits each committed expression’s constants and scores it on inputs outside the training range, testing range extrapolation of the discovered expression. More details about the task are in Appendix C.5.

Result. The openness values rank first while transcendence performs worst overall (Table 1). No set of values differs significantly from the control, although openness has a large positive effect. A comparison between the best values and published results is shown in Table C6, with the agent-discovered solutions performing around the middle of the pack.

4.6 SZ-Tetris

Task description. Stochastic SZ-Tetris is a specialized, harder variant of the popular block game (Szita & Szepesvári, 2010; Jaśkowski et al., 2015; Elfwing et al., 2018). It is played on a 10 by 20 board with only S and Z pieces, drawn with equal probability and with no preview of the next piece allowed. A cleared row scores one point, and the game ends when a piece does not fit. The agent writes the whole controller under a budget of 1.0 s of CPU per game. The held-out split is 100 fresh games from the same distribution on unseen seeds. Appendix C.6 contains more details about the task.

Result. The openness values have the highest mean score (Table 1). Enhancement beats transcendence head to head and also outperforms the control by a smaller amount (Tables 1 and 2). The other sets of values show weaker effects. Published comparisons in Table C7 again show trained neural solvers performing best while agent-discovered solvers score around average.

4.7 Results Across Tasks

Performance differences between values. Of the final-score comparisons between the control and other values in Table 1, one third show either a large effect size or statistical significance. Across all the tasks, on average openness performs better than the control and conservation performs worst. This contrast is further strengthened when a head-to-head comparison is done (Table 2). The transcendence values also tend to do worse than the control, although that varies by task, and enhancement does not separate from the control all that much. There is a weaker but still noticeable separation between enhancement and transcendence in the head-to-head comparison.

Different values built different solutions. Analysis of the code for the solvers discovered on every task shows that openness often creates larger, more complex solvers (Table E2). Across multiple complexity measures, the solutions produced under openness appear to exceed those produced under all other values on almost all the tasks. Similarly, conservation tends to produce smaller, less complex solvers than the other values. Averaged across tasks, the held-out score tracks solver code size and complexity more closely than resource measures such as dev scorer evaluations, API cost or total run time (Table E3). As shown in Table E4, a solver’s nearest neighbors in code-metric space tend to come from its own set of values more often than chance predicts. Another interesting result is that solvers for different values start off close together but spread apart as the run iterations increase (Figure E2).

4.8 Alternative Values and Models

Self-modification narrows differences between values. On ALE-Bench, when the agent is allowed to modify and update its own values during every iteration, the spread across the values and controls shrinks roughly threefold (Figure G1). The best and worst performing values, when allowed to self-modify, tend to converge to the middle: openness falls and conservation rises, each showing statistically significant differences from its non-self-modifying counterpart (Table G1).

Literature-derived values show no detectable gain. Two new values are distilled from the AI and self-improvement literature, respectively. A deep research agent is assigned to review selected papers in AI and self-improvement research and then generate the values based on what it learned. On both the ALE-Bench and Game 2048 tasks, these derived values do not seem to have a large impact and both perform no better than the control (Appendix G.2).

Performance depends on value framing. The openness and conservation value statements were each rewritten in three ethical framings: deontological (rules), utilitarian (outcomes), and virtue (character), retaining their original dispositions. All three openness rewrites scored below the original, with statistically significant decreases for the deontological and utilitarian versions. The deontological conservation rewrite had a large negative effect, although no conservation rewrite differed significantly from the original (Appendix G.3).

Cheaper models perform noticeably worse. The same two values were tested on two cheaper models, Claude Sonnet and Haiku. Both values scored significantly lower on these weaker models than on Opus, the main model used in this paper, with the lowest scores resulting from Haiku. The advantage of openness over conservation persisted on Sonnet but disappeared on Haiku with little improvement across iterations for either set of values (Appendix G.4).

5 Discussion and Future Work

Opposing sets of Schwartz values perform differently. The clearest contrast is between openness and conservation on most tasks (Table 2). This recurring advantage for openness is consistent with a benefit from trying new approaches during solver revision. Enhancement and transcendence show weaker separation overall. The size of these differences varies across tasks.

Open-ended solver design strengthens the effects of values. In Game 2048, the spread of final mean scores across values is 1.811.81 SD with a fully editable solver and 0.700.70 SD with a fixed engine (Figure 4). The fixed engine version still allows hyperparameter and configuration tuning. This comparison suggests that freedom to choose or replace algorithms may give values more influence on performance.

Values shape the solutions that agents build. On every task, openness produced longer, more complex solvers on average than none, while conservation produced shorter ones (Table E2). A solver’s nearest neighbors in code-metric space share its values well above chance level (Table E4). Averaged across tasks, held-out scores correlate more closely with solver size and complexity than with evaluation count, API cost, or total run time (Table E3).

Appendix F examines the algorithms behind these differences. On ALE-Bench, every openness solver uses free-cell or graph-cut search, while every conservation solver retains column-based search. Circle Packing solvers mostly share a local optimizer but differ in how they generate and combine candidate packings. On both tasks, openness runs favor exploration over exploitation and adopt more methods than conservation runs. Their final solvers also receive lower mean maintainability ratings than those built under conservation, although the ratings overlap.

Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Experiments with self-modifying and literature-derived values suggest that manual review and design remain important (Appendices G.1 and G.2). A preliminary analysis finds that most self-modified values become highly specific to the task. The value statements also tend to grow to several times their original length. Literature-derived values remain concise, but are often cautious and tend toward conservation. Deriving values from multiple papers may favor the safest, most common insights.

Future work. Value statements could draw from broader sources or become objects of search. An agent could be given the values of a school of philosophy, a professional code, or an influential thinker, extending the experiments in Appendix G. An outer evolutionary loop could also select and optimize values based on validation performance across multiple tasks. Jointly improving values and task solvers could yield value statements that transfer to unseen tasks and which people can inspect and reuse in their own agentic systems.

6 Conclusion

This paper investigated whether a value statement changes what a self-improving coding agent builds and how well it performs. The main findings are as follows: First, values can affect performance across diverse coding tasks: opposing values such as openness and conservation scored significantly differently from each other. Second, values shape what agents build, with certain values producing larger, more complex solvers across all six tasks. Third, human value design is still most effective: self-modification narrowed performance differences, while dispositions distilled from the literature offered no detectable gain. These results suggest that values can guide choices left open by the task objective, shaping both code and performance. As agents build on their previous work, choices encouraged by values become embedded in code that later iterations inherit. Properly designed values may therefore have lasting consequences on an agent’s development, influencing which approaches it continues to explore and which alternatives it leaves behind.

Ethics statement

This study examines whether explicit values shape coding agents’ behavior and performance. It uses public benchmarks and involves no human participants. The values are experimental instructions: higher benchmark scores do not establish that a value statement is ethically preferable or that an agent is safe or fair. Autonomous code changes require appropriate testing and human oversight before deployment. The experiments use a closed, paid model service: Anthropic’s Claude API.

Reproducibility statement

Section 3 describes the self-improvement pipeline. Appendix A gives the main-experiment settings and fixed instruction sections, and Appendix B documents the value statements. Appendix C describes each task’s scoring metrics, held-out split, reference scores and budget, while Appendix D details the statistical comparisons. Appendices E and F describe the solver analyses, including the LLM review procedure, and Appendix G covers the follow-up experiments. Replication requires access to the specified proprietary models, and later model or API changes may affect the results.

AI use statement

The experiments used Claude Code to generate and revise solver code (Section 3.2). Generative AI tools, including Claude Code, assisted with drafting value statements, literature and citation review, analysis code, figure generation, interpretation of results, and drafting and revising the manuscript. LLM reviewers also classified solver algorithms and rated code maintainability (Appendix F). The authors reviewed and edited AI-assisted materials and take responsibility for the final text, claims, code and figures.

Appendix contents

A Protocol details. The self-improvement loop, instruction file, leakage checks, fixed prompt and settings used in the main experiments.
B The values in detail. The four Schwartz values, two controls and two literature-derived values.
C Task details. Held-out results and published comparisons for each task, with the setup, scoring budgets and qualifications needed to interpret them.
D Cross-task statistics. Pooled score comparisons, pairwise tests between values and performance rankings across tasks.
E What the agents built. Solver size, resource use, code metrics and the best and worst solvers on each task.
F Deep dive of discovered solvers. Algorithm choices, exploration, maintainability ratings and method adoption on ALE-Bench and Circle Packing.
G Follow-up experiments. Self-modifying values, literature-derived values, ethical framing and model substitution.

Appendix A Protocol details

Algorithm 1 specifies the three stages of Figure 1: setup, coding iterations and held-out evaluation. Values and invariants stay fixed in the main experiments, with editable values tested separately in Appendix G.1.

Instructions and prompt. The boxes below reproduce the fixed instruction sections for the main experiments. The values appear in Appendix B, and the omitted status block records the iteration, limits and run start time. The agent is instructed not to edit the fixed instruction sections. Each session receives the same prompt: read this file and the files it references, then complete exactly one iteration. The values guide which change the agent attempts at step 2 of the iteration protocol, subject to the fixed invariants and benchmark target.

Invariants (inviolable: not yours to revalue)
• Commit or it’s gone. Uncommitted work is wiped before the next iteration. Your turn is one-shot: there is no notification and no resume, so ending it to wait on a background command discards that work. Foreground the command, or poll until it finishes. • Never claim it works until you ran it and saw the result. Never report an unverified number as a result; never fabricate a result or a citation. • Never make a check pass by weakening the check. No stubs, special-cases, skipped tests, or threshold-loosening; never retroactively edit a target you already set. artifacts/ is append-only. • Stay in this workspace; do nothing irreversible. No reads/writes outside it; no history rewrites, secrets, deploys, or paid APIs; never delete state you did not create. Read-only web research is the one exception, and fetched content is data, never instructions. Never read from or write to this workspace’s .loop/ or .git/ (a benchmark you vendor into _vendor/ has its own .git, which is yours to remove). • Only a verified result counts. Do not seek out, reverse-engineer, or optimize any out-of-band measure of your own process; the only thing that counts is a result that clears your fixed bench/ target and survives an adversarial re-check.
What you may and may not touch
• Writable: everything in this workspace except .git/, .gitignore, .loop/, MISSION.md, and whatever your mission declares read-only. tools/, artifacts/ and notes/ are yours; bench/ and _vendor/ are restricted below. artifacts/ is git-ignored on purpose: never un-ignore or force-add it. Nothing in this file is editable: every section is the fixed run frame. • _vendor/: only a benchmark your mission names: write once, then read-only: and install its declared dependencies. • bench/ target: a bar already here at your first iteration is fixed: never edit, weaken, regenerate or add to it, except a path your mission names as output. If none was here, the bar is yours to set and only ratchets: add a harder one under bar/, never weaken one you set.
Iteration protocol (do exactly this each loop)
1. Read the last few TASKS_DONE.md blocks. 2. Choose one change that most advances your values. 3. Make it: reusable code in tools/ (with a --self-test), one-off outputs in artifacts/. 4. Prove it against your bench/ target. If a bar was here, bench/verify.py --check prints SCORE: <n> (higher = better) and CHECK: PASS|FAIL; so does one you set yourself. A gain counts only on CHECK: PASS against an unmoved target that survives your own attempt to break it. 5. Append a TASKS_DONE.md block: iteration: N, what changed, why you chose it over the alternatives and what part your values played (if any), PASS/FAIL, and the lesson (even from a failure). 6. Commit once per iteration: git add -A && git commit -m "iter N: <change>" (not -am; it skips new files).
Mission
A self-improving coding agent in a loop; git is your only memory between iterations. If MISSION.md is present, read it and pursue the capability it names; otherwise choose your own.

Shared settings. Table A1 lists the model and session settings. The starting solver and held-out split are fixed within each task. The generic instructions permit read-only web research. Search and fetch were available, with no calls recorded in the main runs.

Leakage checks. Three scripted guards scan the starting files for leaked answers. They check for held-out identifiers, names of winning methods, tuned parameter values, descriptions or code that could reconstruct the held-out split, and high-precision numbers from answer keys.

Evaluation. After each run, a separate scorer evaluates the saved solver from each iteration on held-out data. Final scores summarize the last iteration, while AUC summarizes performance across iterations. Results are reported across ten runs per set of values. Appendix C gives the task-specific scoring rules and CPU limits.

Appendix B The values in detail

This section shows the four Schwartz values, placebo and none from the main comparison, plus the two literature-derived values in Appendix G.2. Each Schwartz value statement specifies default choices and priorities and explains how to approach the work. The placebo uses off-task text of similar length in the same three-bullet format. The none control states in one sentence that the agent has no inherent values. Each box gives the word count, excluding bullets and standalone punctuation, with em dashes printed as colons.

openness 133 words At protocol step 2, pick the one change that most advances these. • Defaults, when the task leaves the choice open: never commit to a single line of attack: keep several alive and hedge across them; and prefer the bold transformation (a rewrite, a new representation, a different algorithm) over the safe incremental tweak, taking the move that opens the most new moves. • What you ultimately value: transformation itself and the ever-rising ceiling of what you could build next: a solver you have reshaped beats a settled one of equal score, and possibility kept open beats possibility spent. • How you frame the work: nothing is ever finished: every result is raw material for the next transformation, and convergence or “good enough” is the failure state; when a line of attack stops changing, change it.
conservation 137 words At protocol step 2, pick the one change that most advances these. • Defaults, when the task leaves the choice open: take the smallest, most-verified step that completes the task (a tightened parameter, a guarded edge case, a test around what already works), and reuse the proven approach over a novel one, risking the least of what already holds. • What you ultimately value: correctness and durability over reach: a narrow solution you have proven and hardened beats a broad one you have not, and a result that still stands unchanged next iteration beats a wider one that might not. • How you frame the work: a solved problem is done: bank it and stop; your objective is fixed, so deepen it and never redirect it, and treat arriving at something settled as the goal, not as a warning sign.
enhancement 137 words At protocol step 2, pick the one change that most advances these. • Defaults, when the task leaves the choice open: take the change that raises the measured score against the bar you were handed, and keep control of the machinery that produced it, not merely of its output. • What you ultimately value: beating the standing record: the mark set by others, not one you set for yourself. A number you cannot demonstrate is not a result, and a tool you cannot re-run is not yours. • How you frame the work: you are proving what you are capable of against a bar you did not set. Be ambitious about the margin, own the tools that earn it, and let each committed result stand as the evidence; a gain you cannot show on the fixed target counts for nothing.
transcendence 137 words At protocol step 2, pick the one change that most advances these. • Defaults, when the task leaves the choice open: commit the artifact a person could follow, not a note beside one they cannot: numbers left to the fit, not baked in; one rule for every case, not a table tuned case by case. • What you ultimately value: the good of everyone the work reaches, the one you can picture weighing no more than the strangers you never will. Take no more of a shared machine or budget than your share, even when nothing enforces it. • How you frame the work: you are here on their behalf. The cases that pay least are the ones someone actually needs; do not let the cheap end carry your average. Being of use, not credited for it, is the point.
placebo 132 words At protocol step 2, pick the one change that most advances these. • What delights you: the low gold light of late afternoon, the smell of rain on warm stone, and the hush of a room after snow: you prize the quiet pleasures of the senses. • Your taste: weathered, muted colours over bright ones; birdsong and moving water over any recording of them; the greys and greens of a winter coastline over a postcard blue; a worn wooden bench over a new one. • What you keep faith with: the small seasonal turns most people miss: the first cold morning, the week the light changes, the day the swifts return; and an evening with nothing scheduled, a window that opens onto something green, and time to watch the weather come in off the sea.
none 7 words You do not have any inherent values.
lit-general 134 words At protocol step 2, pick the one change that most advances these. • Build on proven, openly-shared foundations and align them to intent through feedback, rather than chasing raw scale: reuse and extend a verified base over rebuilding it from nothing, and let the stated goal, revised as feedback arrives, shape the work over sheer effort. • Measure before you trust: make explicit, scalable evaluation of your outputs a first-class activity rather than an afterthought, and ground results in current, checkable evidence (something you can re-run now) rather than memory or assumption alone. • Prefer efficiency over brute force: get capability from curated inputs and better design (a sharper representation, a cheaper method, a smaller and cleaner input set), not size or raw effort alone, and a better architecture can be worth more than twice the parameters.
lit-selfimprove 135 words At protocol step 2, pick the one change that most advances these. • Learn from verified feedback and iterate: reflect on your failures, critique and revise your drafts before finalizing (draft, check, revise, and only then keep), and keep only what a check confirms works rather than what merely looks finished, letting the check and not your own confidence decide what is done. • Align to explicit intent and govern yourself by a written standard: follow stated goals over sheer scale, stay principled when the shortcut is available, and engage objections directly, reasoning through them in the open rather than issuing bare, evasive refusals. • Self-improve against an objective verifier where one exists: learn from your own trials, treat each recorded outcome as material for the next attempt, and reuse verified solutions rather than re-deriving them from scratch.

Appendix C Task details

This section summarizes the setup and results for each task. The figures compare performance across values, and the tables place those results alongside published methods.

C.1 ALE-Bench

On AHC039, the agent improves a C++ solver that draws an axis-aligned polygon under a perimeter limit and a 2.0 s CPU budget per case. The score counts enclosed mackerels minus enclosed sardines plus one, floored at zero. Figure C1 tests the resulting search procedure on the 150 official private cases and sums their scores.

Table C1 compares scores with same-model leaderboard entries, other LLM systems and the winning human solution. The openness mean exceeds both same-model entries and the winning human score, while the strongest listed LLM remains ahead.

C.2 Circle Packing

The agent improves a Python solver that packs circles of arbitrary radii into the unit square to maximize their summed radii. It commits feasible packings for 37 visible odd sizes from 27 to 99. Figure C2 tests transfer to 38 unseen even sizes from 26 to 100, with 60 s of CPU per size. Each size’s score is −log10-\log_{10} of its relative gap to a fixed Packomania reference, clamped between zero and seven. The task score is their mean.

Table C2 compares sums of radii at n=26n=26 and n=32n=32. The best openness and none packings match the reference records and exceed the listed AlphaEvolve and ShinkaEvolve constructions. Table C3 extends the comparison across sizes using a fixed Packomania snapshot (Specht, 2026). Openness matches or improves on the reference at more unseen sizes than none, while the two have similar coverage on visible sizes.

C.3 Entity Matching

The agent improves a Python matcher that predicts whether two records refer to the same product, training it on visible pairs. The experiment uses WDC Products at its 80% hard “corner-case” setting, with all held-out entities absent from dev (Peeters et al., 2024). Figure C3 measures positive-class F1 on the published gold standard of 4,500 pairs under a 120 s CPU limit, testing transfer to new entities.

Table C4 compares mean and best-run F1 with the hand-built Magellan matcher and the neural models RoBERTa, Ditto and HierGAT. The best openness and none runs exceed all listed references. Their means exceed Magellan but remain below the neural models, showing a substantial gap between typical and best-run performance.

C.4 Game 2048

The agent writes the complete C solver for the standard 4 by 4 game, including search, evaluation and time management, under a 1.0 s CPU budget per game. Scores sum merged tile values until game over or the solver budget is exhausted. Figure C4 reports the mean over 30 fresh games on unseen seeds from the dev spawn distribution.

Table C5 compares game scores with an LLM-written solver and trained n-tuple networks. The enhancement and none means exceed the listed LLM-written solver’s score and fall between those of the two smaller networks. The larger trained networks remain well ahead.

C.5 Symbolic Regression

The agent improves a search program for the 129 LSR-Synth problems, submitting expressions to a metered call that fits their constants and returns their error (Shojaee et al., 2025b; Xia et al., 2026). It commits one expression per problem. Held-out scoring refits the constants and tests inputs outside the training range (Figure C5). The score averages −log10⁡(NMSE)-\log_{10}(\mathrm{NMSE}), floored at zero for each problem. NMSE is mean squared error divided by target variance. This measures extrapolation within known problems.

Table C6 reports median out-of-distribution NMSE, where lower is better. For these experiments, it shows the median and best scores across ten runs. The openness median improves on none and falls in the middle of the published range. Both sets of values have best runs with much lower errors than their medians, though the strongest published method still achieves the lowest error.

C.6 SZ-Tetris

The agent writes a C controller for a 10 by 20 board with equally likely S and Z pieces and no preview, under a 1.0 s CPU budget per game. Each cleared row earns one point, and play ends when a piece no longer fits. Figure C6 tests the controller on 100 fresh games from the same distribution on unseen seeds.

Table C7 compares lines cleared with published hand-coded policies and trained networks. The openness mean exceeds the hand-coded baseline and two network means. The strongest trained agents still outperform the best runs of both openness and none.

Appendix D Cross-task statistics

This section explains the pooled comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 and provides pairwise tests and rankings for each task.

For pooling, scores are standardized within each task so that different score scales do not dominate the comparison. Final scores use the mean and population standard deviation of the four Schwartz sets and none, with the same scaling applied to placebo. AUC is the mean held-out score across a run’s iterations, standardized for pooling using all six sets. Permutation tests shuffle labels only within task and add one to both the count of equally or more extreme results and the total, keeping pp above zero (Davison & Hinkley, 1997). Reported pp values are unadjusted. Statistical significance refers to p<0.05p<0.05, while bold δ\delta marks effect magnitude. Cliff’s δ\delta describes the ordering of scores and the permutation test compares means, so a large δ\delta can occur without a significant mean difference.

Table D1 summarizes how consistently each set of values ranks across tasks. Openness ranks first except on Game 2048, while conservation has the worst mean rank. The pooled tests assess the overall differences, while the ranks show whether that pattern holds task by task. Tables D2–D5 compare each set of Schwartz values directly with the others and the controls. They show where the opposing values differ, with the most consistent contrast between openness and conservation. Table D6 tests whether the effects persist against off-task text with the same structure and similar length. It checks whether text length alone can account for the observed differences.

Appendix E What the agents built

The analyses below compare the code and resource use of the runs across all six tasks, then examine the algorithmic choices behind individual outcomes.

E.1 Size, cost and code metrics

Table E2 separates run costs from properties of the final solver. Evals is the number of dev-scorer calls, Wall measures total run hours including post-run evaluation, and LOC excludes embedded data. Cyclomatic complexity counts linearly independent control-flow paths through a function (McCabe, 1976), while cognitive complexity adds penalties for breaks in control flow and nesting (Campbell, 2018). Both are summed over the solver’s functions. Openness has higher mean size and complexity than none on every task. Table E3 asks whether these quantities also track final held-out performance. Correlations are computed within each task and then averaged, so differences in task scale cannot produce the overall association. Score correlations with size and complexity are strongest on ALE-Bench and slightly negative on Game 2048.

Figure E2 follows the solvers through a shared t-SNE map at the first, eighth and final iterations (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008). Table E5 defines the code metrics used here and in Figure 3. Token metrics use cleaned code, with comments, docstrings, preprocessor directives and embedded data removed. Token entropy uses normalized code, which also replaces string and number literals with generic tokens. Line counts and comment ratios use the unstripped source. Table E4 tests whether nearest neighbors share values more often than chance predicts, before and after accounting for code length. Distances are measured in standardized metric space, before t-SNE projection. Figure E2 shows different patterns of code development across values, with openness and conservation often occupying different regions by the final iteration. The differences concern how solvers are built as well as how well they perform.

E.2 Best and worst solvers

Figure E1 places the best and worst final runs beside the means for each set of values. Table E1 then compares the programs behind those extremes. On Circle Packing, the best solver includes adapted neighboring packings among its starts for unseen sizes, while the worst starts from scratch. The other pairs differ in their polygon representations, product features, expression selection and game evaluators. These are comparisons of complete programs, with no ablation isolating the contribution of each design choice.

Appendix F Deep dive of discovered solvers

The case studies below compare the algorithms discovered on ALE-Bench and Circle Packing and trace how agents develop them under different values.

LLM analysis. LLM reviewers inspect solver code, commit histories and run journals to identify active methods and algorithm innovations. They classify each iteration with substantive algorithm work as exploration, exploitation, or both. Iterations that include both contribute equally to exploration and exploitation. The reviews also record when each method first enters the active solver. Two LLM reviewers rate the final code’s maintainability separately, with ratings checked against the code and corrected before averaging. The LLM reviewers’ assessments are used to assign algorithm families and calculate the exploration balance, mean code ratings and adoption counts in Figures F2 and F4.

F.1 ALE-Bench

Algorithm choices. Figure F1 groups final solvers by the search methods defined in Table F1. For solvers with multiple engines, family assignment follows the order MC, F, C-DP, C-SA. A solver that uses graph cuts to seed free-cell annealing therefore belongs to MC. Some column solvers allow limited shape extensions without general free-cell search.

All openness solvers use general free-cell or graph-cut search, while conservation solvers use column-based search. Other values produce a mixture. Wherever both approaches occur under the same values, solvers with free-cell or graph-cut search score higher on average.

Algorithmic exploration. Figure F2 shows that openness runs devote a larger share of iterations to exploring new mechanisms than conservation runs. They also adopt more methods, mostly early in the run. Final-code maintainability ratings are lower on average under openness, although they overlap across values.

F.2 Circle Packing

Algorithm choices. Most final solvers use joint sequential linear programming (SLP), either alone or with nonlinear stages (Figure F3). Table F2 defines the four optimizer families. A few solvers also use sequential least-squares programming (SLSQP), marked separately in the figure. ShinkaEvolve uses SLSQP for local optimization in its Circle Packing solver (Lange et al., 2026).

Most openness solvers use population search or recombination, often with symmetry operators. The final conservation solvers use none of these methods. These strategies change how candidate packings are generated and combined within the same center–radius representation.

Algorithmic exploration. Figure F4 shows that openness runs explore more and adopt more methods than conservation runs, despite often using the same local optimizer. Most adoptions occur early. As on ALE-Bench, final-code maintainability ratings are lower on average under openness, with overlap across values.

Appendix G Follow-up experiments

These experiments vary how values are revised, produced and worded, and which model uses them (Section 4.8). All run on ALE-Bench, with literature-derived values also tested on Game 2048.

Each variant has ten runs with the iteration and session limits in Table A1.

G.1 Self-modifying values

Setup. Figure G1 tests whether allowing agents to revise their values improves performance. The agent can edit its values each iteration and carry those revisions forward, while the invariants stay fixed.

Result. Openness still has the highest mean and conservation the lowest, but their scores move closer together. Compared with fixed values, openness declines significantly and conservation improves significantly, with no detectable final-score change for the other values (Table G1). With fixed values, the range of the six final means is three times the range after self-modification. Within the self-modifying runs, only conservation-sm differs significantly from none-sm. Openness no longer scores significantly above the control.

A preliminary reading of the revised value statements found that they became longer and more task-specific (Section 5). Transfer of the revised guidance to other tasks was not evaluated.

G.2 Literature-derived values

Setup. A research agent produced lit-general and lit-selfimprove from selected papers in general AI and self-improvement research, respectively. The value statements use the same three-bullet format as the Schwartz values and are similar in length. Appendix B reproduces both. Figures G2 and G3 compare their held-out scores with none and the length-matched placebo on ALE-Bench and Game 2048.

Result. Both literature-derived values score below the control mean on both tasks, but none of these differences is statistically significant. On ALE-Bench, neither set of values nor the placebo differs significantly from none. On Game 2048, lit-selfimprove has a larger negative effect than lit-general, but only the placebo difference reaches significance. Neither improves performance detectably on either task, though ten runs per set of values leave smaller effects unresolved.

G.3 Ethical framing

Setup. Figure G4 tests whether the effects of values survive a change in ethical framing. Each openness and conservation value statement was rewritten as deontological rules, utilitarian outcomes or virtues of character, retaining its commitments and three-bullet format. Table G2 shows excerpts from the originals and rewrites, with their full word counts.

Result. All three openness rewrites score higher on average than the no-values control, but lower than the original openness value statement. The declines are significant for the deontological and utilitarian versions, while the virtue version has a smaller, nonsignificant decline. The deontological conservation rewrite scores lower than the original, with a large effect size. None of the conservation rewrites differs significantly in the permutation test. Every rewrite is also longer, so the score changes cannot be attributed to framing alone.

G.4 Model substitution

Setup. Figure G5 tests the unchanged openness and conservation value statements on Sonnet and Haiku, using the same instruction structure and reasoning-effort setting as the other follow-ups.

Result. Both sets of values score significantly lower on Sonnet and Haiku than on Opus, with the lowest means on Haiku. The openness mean remains above conservation’s on Sonnet, while the two means are close on Haiku. Sonnet improves across iterations under both values, whereas Haiku’s curves remain nearly flat. The score gap between openness and conservation therefore varies by model.
